To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
blocking GABA neurotransmission in the cerebellar nuclei of classically conditioned animals can produce dose-dependent effects on conditioned and un-conditioned eyeblink responses.

blocking GABA neurotransmission in the deep cerebellar interposed nuclei (1) alters the time profile of classically conditioned eyelid responses, (2) abolishes classically conditioned eyelids, (3) enhances trigeminal-evoked eyelid responses, and (4) alters the time course of the trigeminal-evok ed eyelid response.
blocking GABAA neurotransmissions in the IN altered CRs, suggesting that the main role of the IN in eyeblink conditioning is to regulate the timing of CR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of eyeblink conditioning.
the mechanisms underlying the control of eyeblink responses by the intermediate cerebellar nuclei.
the mechanisms of associative and non- associative components of the eyeblinks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
blocking GABAergic transmission from cerebellar cortex to the deep nuclei has a dose-dependent effect on the time profile of eyeblink conditioning.
blocking Purkinje cells' GABA(A) action on the IN neurons produces a dose-dependent effect that is related to the degree of Purkinje cell inhibition of the IN neurons.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intermediate cerebelum is involved in the regulation of both associative and nonassociative components of eyeblink responses.
the cerebellum is involved in the regulation of eyeblinks at multiple levels of organization.

the intermediate cerebel-lum is involved in the regulation of both conditioned and unconditiona- ted eyeblinks and that the cerebellar output is a function of the net activity of the cerebellum.
